questions.prompt: How does the MCP specification describe MCP?

options.text: As one AI vendor's private tool format that only its own models can use.
options.explanation: The specification describes an open protocol, not a private format.

options.text: As an open protocol connecting LLM apps to outside data and tools.
options.explanation: Right. That is why a tool connection built on MCP is not tied to a single AI vendor.

options.text: As a pricing scheme for AI models that sets what each token costs.
options.explanation: MCP is about connecting tools and data. It has nothing to do with prices.

questions.prompt: According to Anthropic's model deprecations page, what happens to requests sent to a retired model?

options.explanation: Right. The page says requests to retired models will fail, so apps need to move before the retirement date.

options.text: They are quietly sent to the newest model.
options.explanation: The page does not say this. It says requests fail.

options.text: They keep working at a higher price.
options.explanation: The page describes retired models as no longer available for use.

questions.prompt: What do Anthropic's Claude Code docs say about MCP servers?

options.text: They only work inside Claude Code, and no other AI client or tool can connect to them.
They aren't specific to Claude Code; setup notes may name Claude Desktop or Cursor.
options.explanation: Right. This is a sign that an MCP server can serve more than one AI client.

options.text: They must be rebuilt from scratch for every new AI client that you add.
options.explanation: The docs describe servers as shared across clients, not rebuilt for each.
